title: Environmental Stress
summary: Stress is any physical or emotional state that causes bodily or mental tension. Environmental stress is an undesirable transaction between the person and the environment; the demands made by environmental factors are its sources (stressors). Environment includes the physical world and the socio-cultural surroundings; environmental psychology deals with the effects of environment on behaviour.

(a) Humans subjugated to nature: nature rules human beings; sun, moon, trees and animals are worshipped and feared; still held in some cultures. (b) Humans control over nature: science and technology (kidney transplant, open-heart surgery, genetic engineering, vegetables available all year) gave control, but earthquakes, global warming, ozone depletion and nuclear power threats show the need for balance. (c) Symbiotic relationship: human beings and nature are interdependent and neither is sufficient in itself; humans must feel a duty towards nature and not exploit it blindly, since resources such as oil and coal are non-replenishable. It recognises our limitations and the natural interdependence.

Pollution is an undesirable change in the physical, chemical or biological characteristics of air, land and water that may harmfully affect life, largely from human activities and caused by pollutants (substances foreign to the medium). Types: air pollution, water pollution, noise pollution, crowding and greenhouse effect.

Air pollution: an imbalance in air quality that adversely affects living organisms, due to excess gases (carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxide, sulphur dioxide) and suspended particulate matter (SPM) including lead. The Bhopal gas tragedy (methyl isocyanate) is an example. Effects: eye, nose and throat irritation, respiratory and cardiovascular problems, hypertension, asthma, neurological problems, early deaths, epilepsy, memory disturbance and visual and auditory impairments. Sources: power consumption, industrialisation, vehicular traffic, burning of refuse and garbage, smoking, cutting trees for construction.

Water pollution: addition of excess undesirable substances to water making it harmful to human, animal and aquatic life. Causes: domestic and human waste water, industrial waste water and agricultural run-off. Diseases: diarrhoea, intestinal worms, hepatitis A and B; ten per cent of all diseases and twenty per cent of communicable diseases in India are water-related; the Yamuna in Delhi and the Ganga at Kanpur are examples.

Noise pollution: intensity, loudness, timbre or pitch of sound that causes physical discomfort or is unwanted. Annoyance depends on familiarity and attitude, not intensity alone; people habituate. Effects: health hazards (nervousness, sleeplessness, irritability, depression, asthma, impaired eardrums, hearing loss, cardiac changes, loss of concentration), aggression and reduced altruism, disrupted communication, poorer performance and job satisfaction, noisy classrooms lower attention and academic performance, and accidents.

Crowding: subjective discomfort with physiological arousal, loss of control over social interaction and negative perception of space. Density is the objective number of persons per square kilometre; crowding is the experience, which depends on relationship with the people, duration, physical context and meaning (a marriage party versus an overcrowded bus; friends versus strangers). Effects: crime (pick-pocketing, snatching in rush hours), overcrowding in prisons (violent criminals need more personal space; riots) and psychiatric institutions (assaults), raised blood pressure and heart rate, illness, anger, aggression, apathy, social withdrawal and learned helplessness.

Greenhouse effect and global warming: waste, burning fossil fuels and coal, deforestation, forest fires and CFCs release carbon dioxide, methane and CFCs which trap the sun's heat like a glass greenhouse; consequences: storms and weather extremes, melting of polar ice caps, rising sea level (about one inch every five years; three Maldives islands under water), tsunamis, disrupted agriculture; a rise of about 3.5 degrees Fahrenheit by 2100 is estimated. It can be reversed by reducing carbon dioxide emissions, planting trees and banning CFCs (a ban by fifty nations has helped the ozone layer, expected to recover in 50–100 years).

The Brundtland Commission (World Commission on Environment and Development) defined it as development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. It means preserving stocks of resources, environmental and exhaustible. Worry comes from wasteful consumption and use of non-renewable resources (coal, oil); nature's assimilating capacity is limited. Environment has no natural boundaries. What we can do: conserve water, use public transport, use paper or cotton bags, save electricity, compost, reduce, reuse and recycle, plant trees, buy energy-efficient appliances, use phosphate-free detergents.

Plato's reply in his student's shop shows the difference: a want is a wishful thing and desires are endless; a need is something without which one cannot survive (air, food, water, clothes, house, medicine) and professional needs (a writer's pen). Buying unneeded things wastes money and exploits resources; simple living means fewer wants with inward richness – joy, contentment, beauty and wisdom.

objective: An undesirable transaction between the person and the environment.
Name the three models of human–environment relationship.
Humans subjugated to nature, humans control over nature, and symbiotic relationship.
An undesirable change in the physical, chemical or biological characteristics of air, land and water that may harm life.
Name the five types of environmental stressors.
Air pollution, water pollution, noise pollution, crowding and greenhouse effect.
Name any two major air pollutants.
Carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxide, sulphur dioxide, suspended particulates including lead (any two).
Name any two sources of water pollution.
Domestic waste water, industrial waste water, agricultural run-off (any two).
Differentiate density and crowding in one line each.
Density is the objective number of persons per unit area; crowding is the subjective feeling of discomfort.
Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
Differentiate want and need in one line each.
A want is a wishful desire without end; a need is something essential for survival.
objective4: Name the model: (i) nature is worshipped; (ii) science and technology dominate; (iii) interdependence; (iv) which model recognises our limitations?
(i) Humans subjugated to nature. (ii) Humans control over nature. (iii) Symbiotic. (iv) Symbiotic relationship.
Identify the effect: (i) hearing loss; (ii) disrupted communication; (iii) pick-pocketing in rush hour; (iv) rising sea level.
(i) Noise pollution. (ii) Noise pollution. (iii) Crowding. (iv) Greenhouse effect (global warming).
Name four ways to help the environment.
Conserve water; use public transport; plant trees; reduce, reuse and recycle; save electricity (any four).
Crime, aggression, raised blood pressure, social withdrawal, learned helplessness (any four).
vsa: The physical world and the social and cultural surroundings in which we live and interact.
Humans and nature are interdependent; neither is self-sufficient and humans must not exploit nature blindly.
Name two health effects of air pollution.
Respiratory problems, asthma, cardiovascular problems, eye problems, early deaths (any two).
Why do people habituate to noise?
Familiarity and attitude reduce annoyance so they feel less discomfort over time.
Why does crowding differ in a marriage party and an overcrowded bus?
Density may be equal but the relationship with people, duration and meaning differ, so experience differs.
Gases such as carbon dioxide, methane and CFCs trap the sun's heat in the atmosphere, raising temperature.
Why is wasteful consumption a worry for sustainability?
It depletes non-renewable and renewable resources, leaving little for future generations.
sa: Explain the models of human–environment relationship.

Subjugation: nature rules humans and is worshipped; control: science and technology dominate nature but bring global warming and ozone loss; symbiotic: interdependence, duty to nature and avoiding blind exploitation.
Describe air pollution and its sources.
An imbalance in air quality due to gases and particulates; sources are power consumption, industry, vehicles, burning refuse, smoking and cutting trees.
Describe the ill effects of noise pollution.
Health hazards (sleeplessness, irritability, hearing loss), aggression and less helping behaviour, disrupted communication, lower performance and accidents.
Crowding increases crime, causes violence in prisons and psychiatric institutions, raises blood pressure and heart rate and causes anger, aggression, withdrawal and learned helplessness.
Explain the greenhouse effect and its consequences.
Carbon dioxide, methane and CFCs trap heat, causing global warming, melting ice caps, rising sea levels, storms, flooding and agricultural disruption.
How can an individual contribute to a better environment?
By conserving water and electricity, using public transport and cloth bags, composting, recycling, planting trees and buying energy-efficient appliances.
la: Explain any one model of human–environment relationship and the concept of environmental stress.

Environmental stress is an undesirable person–environment transaction. In the symbiotic model, humans and nature are interdependent; blind exploitation of resources like oil and coal causes pollution and threats, so balance and duty to nature are needed.
Describe air pollution and its consequences for health.

Air pollution is imbalance in air quality due to gases and particulates from power use, industry, vehicles, burning and tree cutting. It causes irritation, respiratory and cardiovascular disease, hypertension, asthma, neurological and visual problems and early death; Bhopal is an example.
Describe water pollution, noise pollution and crowding.

Water pollution from domestic, industrial and agricultural waste causes diarrhoea and hepatitis. Noise pollution causes health problems, aggression, communication difficulty and accidents. Crowding is subjective discomfort that raises crime, aggression and illness.
Discuss the greenhouse effect, sustainable development and the need for simple living.

Greenhouse gases cause global warming and rising seas; reversal needs fewer emissions, trees and banning CFCs. Sustainable development meets present needs without harming future generations. Distinguishing needs from wants and simple living reduce exploitation.
